Mating butterflies on Deerweed that is not yet flowering.

Silvery Blue (Glaucopsyche lygdamus) is a small flying insect in the Gossamer-winged Butterflies (Lycaenidae) family with a wing span of 7/8 - 1.25 inches (2.2 - 3.2 cm). It flies February-June. Habitat is varied: coastal scrub and dunes, along trails and roadways, openings in woodland. Adults are avid puddlers. Larval food plants include: lupines, vetches, deerweed, and other legumes. There are many sub species.

"Identification: Upperside of male iridescent silvery blue with narrow dark borders; female darker blue with wide borders. Both sexes have white fringe. Underside gray-brown; both wings with row of white-ringed, round black spots. Subspecies xerces (Boisduval) and pseudoxerces Emmel and Emmel have large white spots with or without black centers.
Life History: Males patrol near the host plants for females. Eggs are laid singly on flower buds and young leaves of the host plants. Caterpillars feed on flowers, seedpods, and young leaves."

Common Checkered-Skipper (Burnsius communis) Formerly in the genus Pyrgus. Mournful Duskywing (Erynnis tristis) is a small, dark skipper in the Duskywing genus of the spread‑wing subfamily Pyrginae within the family Hesperiidae. It has a wingspan of about 32–44 mm. Males are strong hilltoppers and rarely puddles. The wings are mostly brown and black, and the hindwings show a narrow white fringe along the outer margin. The forewings are broader than those of the Funereal Duskywing, giving the butterfly a slightly heavier look in flight. This species is very similar to the Funereal Duskywing, but it can be distinguished by its broader forewing and the lack of the light brown patch along the outer edge that characterizes E. funeralis. Adults fly from early spring through fall and are often seen resting with wings spread flat in sunny openings. The larvae are green with a dark head and feed on various legumes. Adults visit flowers for nectar and are common in open woodlands, chaparral, and disturbed areas.

It has a wingspan of 34–45 mm. The forewings are narrow and pointed, and the hindwings are more triangular with a distinct white fringe along the outer margin. Spread-wing Skippers (Pyrginae) subfamily butterflies stand out because of the way they hold their wings. While most skippers perch with the forewings angled upward and the hindwings flat, spread‑wings rest with all four wings held open and level, more like small moths or brush‑footed butterflies. Their bodies are usually broader and flatter than those of the grass skippers, and many species are dark brown or gray with pale spots, giving them a more subdued look than the bright orange skippers many people first learn to recognize. Their flight is still quick and darting, but often less jittery than the typical “skipping” motion of other skippers.
Spread‑wing skippers are found worldwide, especially in warm and temperate regions. In North America they occur from southern Canada through the United States and deep into Mexico, with the greatest diversity in the Southwest and the tropics. They use a wide range of habitats—woodland edges, chaparral, canyons, meadows, and even gardens—and their caterpillars feed on many different plants, including legumes, mallows, and oaks, depending on the species.
What separates them from the rest of the skipper family is mainly posture and structure: the open‑wing resting position, the broader bodies, and the more moth‑like appearance.

Skippers (Hesperiidae) family butterflies are small, fast‑moving butterflies found almost worldwide, especially in warm and temperate regions. They live in grasslands, meadows, forest edges, chaparral, and even city parks, and many species are common across North America, Europe, Asia, Africa, and Central and South America. What sets them apart from other butterfly families is a combination of body shape, wing posture, and flight style. Skippers have thick, muscular bodies, large heads, and hooked antenna tips, giving them a moth‑like look compared to the slimmer, more delicate shapes of swallowtails, brush‑footed butterflies, or blues. Their wings are usually held at an angle—forewings up, hindwings flat—rather than fully open or fully closed. They also fly in short, rapid bursts, “skipping” from place to place, which is how they got their name. Most species have caterpillars that feed on grasses or herbaceous plants and rest in folded leaves held together with silk.
